Deverbal from ruse (“to rush, charge; to move violently”), probably from Middle Low German rūsen (“to make noise, rumble”). The Low German verb probably belongs to an expressive or onomatopoeic Germanic word family denoting rushing, roaring, or rapid movement, also represented by Middle High German rūschen (“to rush, roar”) and German rauschen (“to rush, roar”). Possibly ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *rūskōną (“to make noise, whiz”), whose deeper origin is uncertain.
Compare Danish rus, Swedish rus and German Rausch (“intoxication, ecstasy”).

1000447.etyen:
Internationalism, borrowed from Latin Tethys, from Ancient Greek Τηθύς (Tēthús), the name of a Titaness associated with water in Greek mythology. The deeper origin of the Ancient Greek name is uncertain. It has been connected with τήθη (tḗthē, “grandmother”), possibly reflecting Tethys's ancient role as an ancestral mother of the gods; an alternative proposal connects it with *kʷeth₂- (“to bubble, foam”).
The moon of Saturn was discovered by Giovanni Cassini in 1684 and was named after the mythological Tethys by John Herschel in 1847. The prehistoric ocean was likewise named after the Titaness

1000703.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Ullinshof (“Ullin's temple”), an old name for the church site and parish. The first element is the genitive of Ullinn, an old divine name traditionally identified with or regarded as a variant of Ullr (“Ull”). The second element is hof (“temple, pagan sanctuary”).
From the early sixteenth century, the second element hof (“temple, pagan sanctuary”) was replaced by -aker (“field, cultivated land”), the form preserved in the place name, while the old genitival first element was retained, producing the modern name Ullensaker.
